# Multiple Linear Regression {#multiple-linear-regression}

## Introduction

Multiple linear regression extends the simple linear regression framework by allowing the response variable to depend on **several explanatory variables simultaneously**. This provides a flexible framework for describing more complex relationships and for constructing predictions using several sources of information.

In many applications, variation in a response cannot be adequately represented using a single explanatory variable. Economic growth, for example, may be related to investment, inflation, interest rates, and exports; academic performance may be related to study habits, socioeconomic characteristics, and prior preparation. Multiple linear regression provides a systematic way to represent these relationships within the same least-squares framework developed previously.

Importantly, the fundamental optimization problem does not change. Simple linear regression, polynomial regression, and multiple linear regression all use the same mathematical machinery. The main difference is the structure of the design matrix.

---

### The General Model

For observation $i$, the multiple linear regression model is

$$
y_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{1,i}
+
\beta_2x_{2,i}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_px_{p,i}
+
e_i,
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

where:

* $y_i$ is the $i$th observation of the **response variable**,
* $\beta_0$ is the **intercept**,
* $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p$ are the coefficients associated with the explanatory variables,
* $x_{1,i},\ldots,x_{p,i}$ are the values of the **explanatory variables** for observation $i$, and
* $e_i$ is the discrepancy between the observed response and the linear component of the model.

At this stage, no probabilistic assumptions are imposed on the errors. The model is treated as a deterministic representation of the observed response using a linear combination of the explanatory variables.

To establish notation that will be used throughout the chapter, define the matrix containing only the explanatory variables as

$$
\mathbf{X}_*
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1 & \cdots & \mathbf{x}_p
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p},
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{x}_j
=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_{j,1}\\
\vdots\\
x_{j,n}
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\qquad
j=1,\ldots,p.
$$

The complete design matrix, including the column associated with the intercept, is

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(p+1)}.
$$

Similarly, define

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
y_1\\
\vdots\\
y_n
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\beta}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0\\
\beta_1\\
\vdots\\
\beta_p
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{e}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
e_1\\
\vdots\\
e_n
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then the model can be written compactly as

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+
\mathbf{e}.
$$

This is exactly the same matrix representation introduced previously for simple linear regression. The difference is that $\mathbf{X}$ now contains several explanatory-variable columns rather than only one.

---

### Interpretation and Objectives

Multiple linear regression has two important objectives in the present part of the course.

1. **Description** — to describe how the response varies with several explanatory variables considered simultaneously.

2. **Prediction** — to use several explanatory variables jointly to construct predictions of the response.

The coefficient $\beta_j$ describes how the linear component of the model changes with $x_j$ when the other explanatory variables are held fixed. In particular,

$$
\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_jx_j+\cdots+\beta_px_p
$$

changes by $\beta_j$ when $x_j$ increases by one unit while the remaining explanatory variables remain unchanged.

This is often called a **partial** or **conditional interpretation** of the coefficient.

However, this interpretation is algebraic rather than automatically causal. Holding the remaining explanatory variables fixed allows us to isolate the contribution of one variable within the fitted linear model, but additional assumptions would be required to interpret that change as the causal effect of modifying the explanatory variable.

Thus, multiple regression allows us to separate the roles played by different columns of the design matrix without requiring a causal interpretation.

---

### Applications and Context

Multiple linear regression is useful whenever several quantities may help describe or predict a response.

For example, economic performance may be represented using explanatory variables such as inflation, unemployment, interest rates, government expenditure, and exports. Rather than fitting a separate regression for each explanatory variable, multiple regression allows all of them to enter the same linear model.

This generalization introduces several mathematical and computational issues that do not arise as clearly in simple regression.

One important issue is **dependence among the explanatory variables**. If two or more columns of $\mathbf{X}_*$ contain very similar information, it may become difficult to distinguish their individual contributions to the fitted model. In extreme cases, exact linear relationships among the columns can cause $\mathbf{X}$ to lose full column rank, so the usual least-squares solution is no longer unique.

Even when the columns are not exactly linearly dependent, strong relationships among them can affect the numerical stability and interpretation of the estimated coefficients. These issues will be studied through the linear algebra of the design matrix.

At this stage, our focus remains on the **least-squares optimization problem**: how the design matrix determines the fitted values, residuals, and coefficient estimates. Statistical inference and the probabilistic interpretation of these quantities will be introduced later.

---

### Connection to Polynomial Regression

We have already encountered a special case of multiple linear regression in **polynomial regression**.

For example, the quadratic model

$$
y_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_i
+
\beta_2x_i^2
+
e_i
$$

can be written using the design matrix

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_1 & x_1^2\\
1 & x_2 & x_2^2\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_n & x_n^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

From the perspective of least squares, the columns containing $x$ and $x^2$ are treated in exactly the same way as two different explanatory-variable columns.

Polynomial regression therefore introduced the essential algebraic structure of multiple regression:

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+
\mathbf{e}.
$$

The difference is conceptual. In polynomial regression, the columns of $\mathbf{X}_*$ are transformations of a single original explanatory variable,

$$
x,\;x^2,\;\ldots,\;x^k,
$$

whereas in general multiple linear regression the columns

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_p
$$

may represent distinct explanatory variables.

Thus, multiple linear regression is the natural generalization of the framework already developed for polynomial regression. The least-squares machinery remains the same; what changes is the number and interpretation of the columns in the design matrix.



















## Example: Modeling GDP

As an applied example, consider the problem of describing and predicting a country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) using several economic indicators. We use the following explanatory variables:

* Inflation rate,
* Unemployment rate,
* Reference interest rate,
* Government spending as a percentage of GDP, and
* Exports as a percentage of GDP.

Unlike simple linear regression, where the relationship between the response and explanatory variable can be displayed in a single scatterplot, multiple regression involves several explanatory variables simultaneously. We therefore begin by examining the variables **pairwise**.

The following code reads the data and produces a scatterplot matrix containing a scatterplot for every pair of variables.

```{r paris-plot-gdp}
# Reads Data
dat <- read.csv(file = "Gdp Data.csv")

# Plot the scatterplots for each pair of variables
pairs(dat)
```

The scatterplot matrix provides an initial visual description of the dataset. In particular, it allows us to examine two types of relationships:

1. the pairwise relationship between GDP and each explanatory variable, and
2. the relationships among the explanatory variables themselves.

The second point becomes especially important in multiple regression. If two explanatory variables are strongly related to each other, then they may contain overlapping information about GDP. Consequently, their coefficients in a multiple regression may behave differently from the coefficients obtained when each variable is considered separately.

The same pairwise relationships can be summarized numerically using correlations.

```{r gdp-cor}
# Computes the correlation between variables
cor(dat)
```

The correlation matrix complements the scatterplot matrix by quantifying the strength and direction of the linear relationships between pairs of variables. Large positive or negative correlations between GDP and an explanatory variable suggest a strong pairwise linear relationship. Large correlations among explanatory variables indicate that some columns of the design matrix may contain similar information.

At this point, these quantities are used only as descriptive tools. The multiple-regression fit will determine how the explanatory variables behave when they are included in the model simultaneously.

---

### Simple Regressions

Before fitting the full multiple regression model, it is useful to fit a separate simple linear regression of GDP on each explanatory variable.

These models answer a different question from the multiple regression. A simple regression describes the relationship between GDP and one explanatory variable **without accounting for the remaining variables**.

For each explanatory variable, the code displays two plots:

* the scatterplot of GDP against the explanatory variable together with its fitted regression line, and
* the residuals from that simple regression.

The first plot helps us visualize the pairwise relationship. The second shows what remains unexplained after fitting that particular straight line.

#### Inflation Rate

```{r gdp-inf-fit}
# Fits with Inflation
outRegInf <- lm(gdp ~ inf, data = dat)
varVal    <- dat$inf
out       <- outRegInf
varNam    <- "Inflation Rate"
# Plots Regression Line and Scatterplot and residuals plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = dat$gdp,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "GDP",
     pch  = 16)
abline(a   = out$coefficients[1],
       b   = out$coefficients[2],
       col = 'red',
       lwd = 2)
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = out$residuals,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     pch  = 16)
abline(h   = 0,
       lwd = 2)
```

The fitted slope describes the pairwise linear relationship between inflation and GDP. It answers how the fitted value of GDP changes with inflation when inflation is the **only explanatory variable included in the model**.

The residual plot shows the differences between the observed GDP values and those predicted using inflation alone. Any remaining structure in the residuals indicates variation in GDP that this simple regression does not represent.

#### Unemployment Rate

```{r gdp-unp-fit}
# Fits with Unemployment
outRegUne <- lm(gdp ~ une, data = dat)
varVal    <- dat$une
out       <- outRegUne
varNam    <- "Unemployment Rate"
# Plots Regression Line and Scatterplot and residuals plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = dat$gdp,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "GDP",
     pch  = 16)
abline(a   = out$coefficients[1],
       b   = out$coefficients[2],
       col = 'red',
       lwd = 2)
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = out$residuals,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     pch  = 16)
abline(h   = 0,
       lwd = 2)
```

This regression describes the relationship between unemployment and GDP when unemployment is considered by itself.

As before, the fitted line summarizes the pairwise linear trend, while the residuals represent the component of GDP that is not captured by that one-variable linear fit.

#### Interest Rate

```{r gdp-int-fit}
# Fits with Interest Rate
outRegInt <- lm(gdp ~ int, data = dat)
varVal    <- dat$int
out       <- outRegInt
varNam    <- "Interest Rate"
# Plots Regression Line and Scatterplot and residuals plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = dat$gdp,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "GDP",
     pch  = 16)
abline(a   = out$coefficients[1],
       b   = out$coefficients[2],
       col = 'red',
       lwd = 2)
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = out$residuals,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     pch  = 16)
abline(h   = 0,
       lwd = 2)
```

The estimated slope now describes the pairwise relationship between the reference interest rate and GDP.

Importantly, this coefficient reflects both the relationship of the interest rate with GDP and any information that the interest rate shares with the other economic variables that have not yet been included in the model.

#### Government Spending

```{r gdp-gov-fit}
# Fits with Government Spending
outRegGov <- lm(gdp ~ gov, data = dat)
varVal    <- dat$gov
out       <- outRegGov
varNam    <- "Government Spending"
# Plots Regression Line and Scatterplot and residuals plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = dat$gdp,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "GDP",
     pch  = 16)
abline(a   = out$coefficients[1],
       b   = out$coefficients[2],
       col = 'red',
       lwd = 2)
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = out$residuals,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     pch  = 16)
abline(h   = 0,
       lwd = 2)
```

This fit examines GDP using government spending as the only explanatory variable.

As with the previous models, the estimated coefficient should be interpreted as a **simple-regression coefficient**. It does not yet describe the relationship between government spending and GDP after accounting for inflation, unemployment, interest rates, or exports.

#### Exports

```{r gdp-exp-fit}
# Fits with Exports
outRegExp <- lm(gdp ~ exp, data = dat)
varVal    <- dat$exp
out       <- outRegExp
varNam    <- "Exports"
# Plots Regression Line and Scatterplot and residuals plot
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = dat$gdp,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "GDP",
     pch  = 16)
abline(a   = out$coefficients[1],
       b   = out$coefficients[2],
       col = 'red',
       lwd = 2)
plot(x    = varVal,
     y    = out$residuals,
     xlab = varNam,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     pch  = 16)
abline(h   = 0,
       lwd = 2)
```

The exports model provides the final pairwise regression. Its slope summarizes how the fitted GDP changes with exports when exports are considered alone.

Taken together, the five simple regressions provide useful benchmarks. They show what each explanatory variable appears to contribute when examined individually. We can now compare these results with a model in which all five explanatory variables are included simultaneously.

***
























### Multiple Regression

The simple regressions answer questions of the form

$$
\text{How is GDP related to } x_j \text{ when } x_j \text{ is used by itself?}
$$

Multiple regression answers a different question. It fits GDP using all explanatory variables simultaneously:

$$
\text{GDP}
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1\text{Inflation}
+
\beta_2\text{Unemployment}
+
\beta_3\text{Interest}
+
\beta_4\text{Government Spending}
+
\beta_5\text{Exports}
+
e.
$$

Each coefficient now describes the change in the fitted linear component associated with one explanatory variable **while the values of the other explanatory variables are held fixed**.

We fit the full model and compare its coefficient estimates with those obtained from the corresponding simple regressions.

```{r gdp-all-ind-com}
outRegAll <- lm(gdp ~ inf + une + int + gov + exp, data = dat)

# Summary All
print("All Independent Variables")
summary(outRegAll)
print("Only Inflation Rate")
summary(outRegInf)
print("Only Unemployment Rate")
summary(outRegUne)
print("Only Interest Rate")
summary(outRegInt)
print("Only Government Spending")
summary(outRegGov)
print("Only Exports")
summary(outRegExp)


# Formats and Show Info Table
tab           <- cbind(outRegAll$coefficients[-1], c(outRegInf$coefficients[2],
                                                     outRegUne$coefficients[2],
                                                     outRegInt$coefficients[2],
                                                     outRegGov$coefficients[2],
                                                     outRegExp$coefficients[2]))
colnames(tab) <- c("All", "Individual")
rownames(tab) <- c("Inflation", "Unemployment", "Interest Rate", "Government Expenditure", "Exports")
knitr::kable(tab)
```

The final table places the multiple-regression coefficients next to the corresponding simple-regression coefficients. These coefficients need not be equal because they describe different fitted relationships.

For example, the simple-regression coefficient for inflation is obtained from a model containing only inflation,

$$
\text{GDP}
=
\beta_0+\beta_1\text{Inflation}+e,
$$

whereas the inflation coefficient in the multiple regression is obtained from a model in which unemployment, interest rates, government spending, and exports are also included.

Therefore, a change in the coefficient after additional explanatory variables are included is not itself surprising. It indicates that the explanatory variables contain overlapping information about the response.

A coefficient may become smaller, larger, or even change sign after the other explanatory variables are included. Such behavior motivates an important question that will be developed mathematically in this chapter:

> How does the relationship among the columns of the design matrix affect the estimated regression coefficients?

This is one of the central differences between simple and multiple regression. In simple regression, there is only one nonconstant explanatory-variable column. In multiple regression, the geometry of the entire collection

$$
\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_p
$$

matters.

The comparison therefore provides a first illustration of why multiple regression cannot be understood simply as several simple regressions performed at the same time. The coefficients are estimated **jointly**, and their values depend on the relationships among all columns of the design matrix.

***

### Summary

This introduction highlights the main ideas that distinguish multiple linear regression from simple linear regression:

1. **Explore the variables jointly.**
   Scatterplot matrices and correlations help identify pairwise relationships between the response and explanatory variables, as well as relationships among the explanatory variables themselves.

2. **Use simple regressions as benchmarks.**
   Fitting GDP separately on each explanatory variable shows how each variable behaves when considered alone.

3. **Fit all explanatory variables simultaneously.**
   Multiple regression estimates the coefficients jointly, so each coefficient describes the role of one explanatory variable while the others are held fixed within the linear model.

4. **Compare simple and multiple regression coefficients.**
   The coefficients can change substantially because the explanatory variables may contain overlapping information. Their values therefore depend on the relationships among all columns of the design matrix.

The central lesson is that multiple regression is **not simply a collection of simple regressions**. It is a single least-squares problem involving several explanatory variables at once.

This makes the structure of the design matrix particularly important. In the following sections, we study how the geometry and algebra of $\mathbf{X}$ determine the coefficient estimates, fitted values, residuals, and behavior of the multiple linear regression model.

***























## Least Squares Estimation

For least squares estimation, we solve the optimization problem

$$
Q(\bgb)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(
y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{j,i}
\right)^2
=
(\by-\bX\bgb)'(\by-\bX\bgb).
$$

The least-squares estimator is therefore defined as

$$
\hat{\bgb}
=
\underset{\bgb}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\;Q(\bgb).
$$

Because the problem has exactly the same matrix form as in simple linear regression, the solution is obtained in the same way.

Suppose that the full design matrix $\bX$ has full column rank,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\bX)=p+1.
$$

Then $\bX'\bX$ is invertible, and the unique least-squares solution is

$$
\hat{\bgb}
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by.
$$

The formula is therefore unchanged from the matrix formulation of simple linear regression. The difference is only the dimension of the coefficient vector. In multiple linear regression,

$$
\bgb
=
\left(
\beta_0,
\beta_1,
\beta_2,
\ldots,
\beta_p
\right)',
$$

and consequently,

$$
\hat{\bgb}
=
\left(
\hat{\beta}_0,
\hat{\beta}_1,
\hat{\beta}_2,
\ldots,
\hat{\beta}_p
\right)'.
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\text{same least-squares optimization}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{same matrix solution}
}
$$

with more explanatory variables. This is why working in matrix form is particularly useful.




















## Properties of the Estimates

As with simple linear regression, we distinguish between the **fitted values** and the **residuals**.

Given the least-squares estimator

$$
\hat{\bgb}
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by,
$$

the fitted values are

$$
\hat{\by}
=
\bX\hat{\bgb},
$$

and the residuals are

$$
\hat{\be}
=
\by-\hat{\by}
=
\by-\bX\hat{\bgb}.
$$

We can also express the fitted values as

$$
\hat{\by}
=
\bX(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by
=
\bH\by,
$$

where

$$
\bH
=
\bX(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'
$$

is called the **hat matrix**, because it transforms $\by$ into $\hat{\by}$. It is also called the **projection matrix**, since it projects $\by$ onto the column space of $\bX$.

The properties of the least-squares solution follow primarily from one important consequence of the normal equations:

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\bgb}
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bX'\hat{\be}=\bzero.
}
$$

When the design matrix includes an intercept, this identity implies that the residuals sum to zero, are orthogonal to every explanatory-variable vector and to the fitted values, and that the mean of the fitted values equals the mean of the observed responses.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-properties-estimates, name="Properties of the Least-Squares Estimates"}
Suppose that the design matrix $\bX$ has full column rank and includes a column of ones for the intercept. Then the least-squares solution satisfies the following properties:

1. Each component of $\hat{\bgb}$ is a linear combination of the entries of $\by$.

2. The sum of the residuals is equal to zero,

   $$
   \sum_{i=1}^n\hat e_i=0.
   $$

3. The residual vector is orthogonal to every explanatory-variable vector,

   $$
   \hat{\be}\perp\bx_j,
   \qquad j=1,\ldots,p.
   $$

4. The residual vector is orthogonal to the fitted-value vector,

   $$
   \hat{\be}\perp\hat{\by}.
   $$

5. The mean of the fitted values equals the mean of the observed responses,

   $$
   \bar y=\overline{\hat y},
   $$

   where

   $$
   \overline{\hat y}
   =
   \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\hat y_i.
   $$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-properties-estimates}

**1. Linearity of the coefficient estimates**

To show that each component of $\hat{\bgb}$ is a linear combination of the entries of $\by$, we need to express the estimator as

$$
\hat{\bgb}=\bA\by
$$

for some matrix $\bA$ that does not depend on $\by$.

Let

$$
\bA
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'.
$$

Then,

$$
\hat{\bgb}
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by
=
\bA\by.
$$

When the design matrix $\bX$ is held fixed, $\bA$ is also fixed. Therefore, each component of $\hat{\bgb}$ is a linear combination of the entries of $\by$.

**2. The normal equations and the sum of the residuals**

The remaining properties follow from the normal equations.

Starting with the least-squares solution,

\begin{align*}
\hat{\bgb}
  &= (\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by
    & \text{least-squares solution} \\
\bX'\bX\hat{\bgb}
  &= \bX'\by
    & \text{multiply by } \bX'\bX \\
\bX'\by-\bX'\bX\hat{\bgb}
  &= \bzero
    & \text{rearrange} \\
\bX'(\by-\bX\hat{\bgb})
  &= \bzero
    & \text{factor } \bX' \\
\bX'\hat{\be}
  &= \bzero
    & \text{def. residuals}.
\end{align*}

This is the central identity from which the remaining properties follow.

Recall that the design matrix includes the column of ones,

$$
\bX
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bones & \bx_1 & \cdots & \bx_p
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\bX'
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bones'\\
\bx_1'\\
\vdots\\
\bx_p'
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Expanding the product $\bX'\hat{\be}$, we obtain

$$
\bX'\hat{\be}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bones'\hat{\be}\\
\bx_1'\hat{\be}\\
\vdots\\
\bx_p'\hat{\be}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The first component of this equality gives

$$
\bones'\hat{\be}=0.
$$

Since $\bones$ is the vector of ones,

$$
\bones'\hat{\be}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\hat e_i.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\sum_{i=1}^n\hat e_i=0.
}
$$

This establishes the second property.

**3. Orthogonality of the residuals to the explanatory variables**

Using the same expansion of the normal equations,

$$
\bX'\hat{\be}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bones'\hat{\be}\\
\bx_1'\hat{\be}\\
\vdots\\
\bx_p'\hat{\be}
\end{bmatrix}
=
\bzero,
$$

we see that its remaining components give

$$
\bx_j'\hat{\be}=0,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,p.
$$

Recall that two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero. Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\be}\perp\bx_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,p.
}
$$

This establishes the third property.

**4. Orthogonality of the residuals to the fitted values**

To show that the residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values, we need to establish that

$$
\hat{\be}'\hat{\by}=0.
$$

Recall that

$$
\hat{\by}
=
\bX\hat{\bgb}.
$$

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
\hat{\be}'\hat{\by}
  &= \hat{\be}'\bX\hat{\bgb}
    & \text{def. fitted values} \\
  &= (\bX'\hat{\be})'\hat{\bgb}
    & \text{transpose rule} \\
  &= \bzero'\hat{\bgb}
    & \text{normal equations} \\
  &= 0.
\end{align*}

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\be}\perp\hat{\by}.
}
$$

This establishes the fourth property.

Notice that the fitted values are linear combinations of the columns of $\bX$. Since the residuals are orthogonal to every column of $\bX$, they must also be orthogonal to the fitted-value vector.

**5. Equality of the means**

Finally, we show that

$$
\bar y=\overline{\hat y}.
$$

Recall from the second property that

$$
\bones'\hat{\be}=0.
$$

Using the definition of the residuals,

\begin{align*}
\bones'\hat{\be}
  &= \bones'(\by-\hat{\by})
    & \text{def. residuals} \\
  &= \bones'\by-\bones'\hat{\by}
    & \text{distributivity} \\
  &= \sum_{i=1}^n y_i-\sum_{i=1}^n\hat y_i
    & \text{def. } \bones \\
  &= n\bar y-n\overline{\hat y}
    & \text{def. means}.
\end{align*}

Since $\bones'\hat{\be}=0$, we obtain

\begin{align*}
n\bar y-n\overline{\hat y}
  &=0\\
n\bar y
  &=n\overline{\hat y}\\
\bar y
  &=\overline{\hat y}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\bar y=\overline{\hat y}.
}
$$

This establishes the fifth property.

Notice that the second and fifth properties depend on the presence of the intercept in the model. Including the intercept ensures that $\bones$ is a column of $\bX$, and therefore the normal equations imply

$$
\bones'\hat{\be}=0.
$$

Without an intercept, the residuals are still orthogonal to the columns of $\bX$, but they are not necessarily orthogonal to $\bones$. Consequently, their sum need not equal zero, and the mean of the fitted values need not equal the mean of the observed responses.
```

</details>

The main result of this subsection is therefore the hierarchy

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\bgb}
=
(\bX'\bX)^{-1}\bX'\by
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bX'\hat{\be}=\bzero.
}
$$

Since the design matrix includes the intercept and all explanatory-variable vectors, the normal equations imply

$$
\boxed{
\bX'\hat{\be}=\bzero
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n\hat e_i=0,\\[6pt]
\hat{\be}\perp\bx_j,\quad j=1,\ldots,p,\\[4pt]
\hat{\be}\perp\hat{\by},\\[4pt]
\bar y=\overline{\hat y}.
\end{cases}
}
$$

Thus, the properties of the residuals and fitted values are direct consequences of a single matrix identity.

























## Multiple $R^2$

As with simple linear regression, we can evaluate the fit of a multiple linear regression model by decomposing the total variability of the response into two components: the variability accounted for by the fitted model and the variability remaining in the residuals.

Throughout this section, we assume that the full design matrix $\mathbf{X}$ includes a column of ones for the intercept and has full column rank.

We begin by defining three sums of squares.

```{definition, def-mlr-total-sum-of-squares, name="Total Sum of Squares"}
The **Total Sum of Squares**, $SS_{tot}$, measures the total variability of the observed responses around their sample mean:

$$
SS_{tot}
=
(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2.
$$
```

```{definition, def-mlr-residual-sum-of-squares, name="Residual Sum of Squares"}
The **Residual Sum of Squares**, $SS_{res}$, measures the variability remaining after fitting the regression model:

$$
SS_{res}
=
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2.
$$
```

```{definition, def-mlr-explained-sum-of-squares, name="Explained Sum of Squares"}
The **Explained Sum of Squares**, $SS_{reg}$, measures the variability of the fitted values around the mean of the observed responses:

$$
SS_{reg}
=
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2.
$$
```

The properties of the least-squares estimates established in the previous section allow us to decompose the total sum of squares into the explained and residual sums of squares.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-sum-of-squares, name="Sum-of-Squares Decomposition"}
Suppose that the multiple linear regression model includes an intercept. Then the least-squares fitted values satisfy

$$
SS_{tot}=SS_{reg}+SS_{res}.
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-sum-of-squares}
We begin with the definition of the total sum of squares. Adding and subtracting the fitted-value vector gives

\begin{align*}
SS_{tot}
  &=
  (\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &=
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}
  +\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}
  +\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &=
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
  \\
  &\quad+
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &\quad+
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
  \\
  &\quad+
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}).
\end{align*}

Recall from the properties of the least-squares estimates that

$$
\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{y}}=0
$$

and, because the model includes an intercept,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\mathbf{1}=0.
$$

Therefore, the first cross-product is

\begin{align*}
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  &=
  \hat{\mathbf{e}}'
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &=
  \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{y}}
  -
  \bar y\hat{\mathbf{e}}'\mathbf{1}
  \\
  &=
  0.
\end{align*}

The other cross-product is its transpose and is also zero. Consequently,

\begin{align*}
SS_{tot}
  &=
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
  \\
  &\quad+
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &=
  SS_{res}+SS_{reg}.
\end{align*}

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
SS_{tot}=SS_{reg}+SS_{res}.
}
$$
```

</details>


This decomposition allows us to define the coefficient of determination for multiple linear regression.


```{definition, def-mlr-multiple-r-squared, name="Multiple Coefficient of Determination"}
Suppose that the multiple linear regression model includes an intercept and that $SS_{tot}>0$.

The **Multiple Coefficient of Determination**, $R^2$, is defined as the proportion of the total variability of the observed responses accounted for by the fitted regression model:

$$
R^2
=
\frac{SS_{reg}}{SS_{tot}}.
$$

Using the sum-of-squares decomposition,

$$
SS_{tot}=SS_{reg}+SS_{res},
$$

we obtain the equivalent expression

$$
R^2
=
1-\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}.
$$
```

The multiple $R^2$ is an in-sample measure of fit. It describes the reduction in squared error achieved by the full regression model relative to the intercept-only model. It does not, by itself, establish predictive performance on new observations.

Using the sum-of-squares decomposition, we also obtain

\begin{align*}
1
  &=
  \frac{SS_{reg}+SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}
  \\
  &=
  R^2+\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
R^2
=
1-\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}.
}
$$

The multiple $R^2$ describes the proportion of the observed variability around $\bar y$ accounted for by the fitted linear model. It is an in-sample measure of fit and does not, by itself, establish causal relationships or predictive performance on new observations.

***

### The Intercept-Only Model

Before expressing $R^2$ using projection matrices, it is useful to introduce a reference model.

Consider a regression model containing only an intercept,

$$
y_i=\beta_0+e_i,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

Its design matrix is

$$
\mathbf{X}_0=\mathbf{1},
$$

and its least-squares problem is

$$
\min_{\beta_0}
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{1}\beta_0)'
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{1}\beta_0).
$$

The least-squares solution is

$$
\hat\beta_0
=
(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1})^{-1}
\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{y}
=
\bar y.
$$

Consequently, the fitted values from the intercept-only model are

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0
=
\bar y\mathbf{1}.
$$

This model assigns the same predicted response, $\bar y$, to every observation. Its residual sum of squares is precisely

$$
SS_{tot}
=
(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
(\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}).
$$

Thus, the total sum of squares can be interpreted as the minimum squared error obtained when we predict the response using only a constant.

Adding explanatory variables enlarges the set of possible fitted-value vectors. This observation will allow us to establish both the range of $R^2$ and its behavior when additional variables are included.

***

### Sums of Squares in Matrix Form

Recall that the hat matrix for the full multiple linear regression model is

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\mathbf{X}
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}',
$$

so that

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}.
$$

Similarly, the hat matrix for the intercept-only model is

$$
\mathbf{H}_0
=
\mathbf{1}
(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1})^{-1}
\mathbf{1}'
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'.
$$

It follows that

$$
\mathbf{H}_0\mathbf{y}
=
\bar y\mathbf{1}.
$$

The matrices $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{H}_0$ project the response vector onto the column spaces of the full and intercept-only design matrices, respectively.

We can now express all three sums of squares using these projection matrices.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-projection-sums-of-squares, name="Sums of Squares Using Projection Matrices"}
Let

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\mathbf{X}
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}'
$$

be the hat matrix of the full multiple linear regression model, where $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank and includes an intercept.

Let

$$
\mathbf{H}_0
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
$$

be the hat matrix of the intercept-only model.

Then the three sums of squares can be written as

$$
\boxed{
SS_{tot}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
\mathbf{y},
}
$$

$$
\boxed{
SS_{res}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
\mathbf{y},
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
SS_{reg}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)
\mathbf{y}.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-projection-sums-of-squares}
We first establish the necessary properties of the projection matrices.

Recall that

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\mathbf{X}
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}'.
$$

Since $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ is symmetric and invertible, its inverse is also symmetric. Therefore,

$$
\mathbf{H}'=\mathbf{H}.
$$

Furthermore,

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{H}^2
  &=
  \mathbf{X}
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \mathbf{X}'
  \mathbf{X}
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \mathbf{X}'
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{X}
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \mathbf{X}'
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{X}
  (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
  \mathbf{X}'
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{H}.
\end{align*}

Thus, $\mathbf{H}$ is symmetric and idempotent.

Consequently, $\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}$ is also symmetric, and

\begin{align*}
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})^2
  &=
  \mathbf{I}-2\mathbf{H}+\mathbf{H}^2
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, $\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}$ is idempotent.

**Residual Sum of Squares**

The residual vector can be written as

\begin{align*}
\hat{\mathbf{e}}
  &=
  \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}-\mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Hence,

\begin{align*}
SS_{res}
  &=
  \hat{\mathbf{e}}'\hat{\mathbf{e}}
  \\
  &=
  \bigl[(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\bigr]'
  \bigl[(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}\bigr]
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
  \mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})^2
  \mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
  \mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
SS_{res}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
\mathbf{y}.
}
$$

**Total Sum of Squares**

For the intercept-only model, we have

$$
\mathbf{H}_0
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'.
$$

This matrix is symmetric. It is also idempotent, since

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{H}_0^2
  &=
  \frac{1}{n^2}
  \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
  \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
  \\
  &=
  \frac{1}{n^2}
  \mathbf{1}
  (\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1})
  \mathbf{1}'
  \\
  &=
  \frac{1}{n}
  \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{H}_0.
\end{align*}

Consequently, $\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0$ is symmetric and idempotent:

$$
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)^2
=
\mathbf{I}-2\mathbf{H}_0+\mathbf{H}_0^2
=
\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0.
$$

Recall that

$$
\mathbf{H}_0\mathbf{y}
=
\bar y\mathbf{1}.
$$

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
SS_{tot}
  &=
  (\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})'
  (\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
  \\
  &=
  \bigl[(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}\bigr]'
  \bigl[(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}\bigr]
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
  \mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
  \mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
SS_{tot}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
\mathbf{y}.
}
$$

**Explained Sum of Squares**

Finally, using the sum-of-squares decomposition,

\begin{align*}
SS_{reg}
  &=
  SS_{tot}-SS_{res}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
  \mathbf{y}
  -
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
  \mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  \bigl[
    (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)
    -
    (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})
  \bigr]
  \mathbf{y}
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'
  (\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)
  \mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
SS_{reg}
=
\mathbf{y}'
(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)
\mathbf{y}.
}
$$
```

</details>

The three sums of squares therefore have a unified matrix representation:

| Sum of squares | Matrix expression |
|---|---|
| Total | $SS_{tot}=\mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}$ |
| Residual | $SS_{res}=\mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}$ |
| Explained | $SS_{reg}=\mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}$ |

Using these identities, the multiple $R^2$ can be written as

$$
\boxed{
R^2
=
1-
\frac{
\mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H})\mathbf{y}
}{
\mathbf{y}'(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}
}.
}
$$

This expression compares the squared error from the full regression model with the squared error from the intercept-only model.

***

### Range of Multiple $R^2$

The optimization interpretation of the two models allows us to establish the possible values of $R^2$.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-r2-range, name="Range of Multiple R-Squared"}
Suppose that the multiple linear regression model includes an intercept and that

$$
SS_{tot}>0.
$$

Then the coefficient of determination satisfies

$$
\boxed{
0\leq R^2\leq 1.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-r2-range}
The residual sum of squares from the full regression model is the minimum value of its least-squares objective:

$$
SS_{res}
=
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})'
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$

Similarly, the total sum of squares is the minimum squared error from the intercept-only model:

$$
SS_{tot}
=
\min_{\beta_0}
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{1}\beta_0)'
(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{1}\beta_0).
$$

Because the full model includes an intercept, every fitted-value vector available to the intercept-only model is also available to the full model.

In particular, the full model can reproduce any constant fit by setting all the explanatory-variable coefficients equal to zero.

Therefore, minimizing over the larger set of possible fitted values cannot produce a larger minimum:

$$
SS_{res}\leq SS_{tot}.
$$

Both sums of squares are nonnegative, so

$$
0\leq SS_{res}\leq SS_{tot}.
$$

Since $SS_{tot}>0$, dividing by $SS_{tot}$ gives

$$
0
\leq
\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}
\leq
1.
$$

Recall that

$$
R^2
=
1-\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
0\leq R^2\leq 1.
}
$$
```

</details>

The condition $SS_{tot}>0$ means that the observed responses are not all identical. When all responses are equal, the usual definition of $R^2$ has a zero denominator and does not apply.

The extreme values have simple interpretations. If $R^2=0$, the full model does not reduce the residual sum of squares relative to the intercept-only model. If $R^2=1$, the full model fits every observed response exactly, so $SS_{res}=0$.

***

### Adding an Explanatory Variable

One consequence of the least-squares formulation is that adding an explanatory variable cannot increase the minimum residual sum of squares when both models are fitted to the same observations.

The additional variable expands the set of possible fitted-value vectors. At worst, the expanded model can reproduce the original fit by assigning a coefficient of zero to the new variable.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-additional-variable-r2, name="Effect of Adding an Explanatory Variable on R-Squared"}
Consider a multiple linear regression model with an intercept and design matrix $\mathbf{X}$. Let its residual sum of squares and coefficient of determination be $SS_{res}$ and $R^2$, respectively.

Now consider an expanded model obtained by adding another explanatory-variable vector $\mathbf{z}$:

$$
\mathbf{X}_+
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{X} & \mathbf{z}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Let $SS_{res,+}$ and $R_+^2$ denote the corresponding quantities for the expanded model, fitted using the same observations.

Then

$$
\boxed{
SS_{res,+}\leq SS_{res}.
}
$$

Furthermore, if $SS_{tot}>0$, then

$$
\boxed{
R_+^2\geq R^2.
}
$$

Thus, adding an explanatory variable cannot decrease the ordinary in-sample $R^2$.
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-additional-variable-r2}
For the original regression model, the residual sum of squares is

$$
SS_{res}
=
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\left\|
\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
\right\|^2.
$$

For the expanded model, introduce the coefficient $\gamma$ associated with the additional explanatory variable $\mathbf{z}$.

Its residual sum of squares is

$$
SS_{res,+}
=
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\gamma}
\left\|
\mathbf{y}
-
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
-
\gamma\mathbf{z}
\right\|^2.
$$

Notice that the expanded optimization problem includes every candidate fitted-value vector from the original problem. We can always recover the original model by choosing

$$
\gamma=0.
$$

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
SS_{res,+}
  &=
  \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta},\gamma}
  \left\|
  \mathbf{y}
  -
  \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
  -
  \gamma\mathbf{z}
  \right\|^2
  \\
  &\leq
  \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \left\|
  \mathbf{y}
  -
  \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
  -
  0\mathbf{z}
  \right\|^2
  \\
  &=
  \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \left\|
  \mathbf{y}
  -
  \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}
  \right\|^2
  \\
  &=
  SS_{res}.
\end{align*}

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
SS_{res,+}\leq SS_{res}.
}
$$

Since both regressions use the same response observations, their total sum of squares is the same.

Provided that $SS_{tot}>0$,

\begin{align*}
R_+^2
  &=
  1-\frac{SS_{res,+}}{SS_{tot}}
  \\
  &\geq
  1-\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}
  \\
  &=
  R^2.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
R_+^2\geq R^2.
}
$$
```

</details>


The inequality need not be strict. For example, if the new explanatory-variable vector is already a linear combination of the columns of $\mathbf{X}$, the expanded model has exactly the same set of possible fitted-value vectors. In this case, adding the variable does not change the residual sum of squares or $R^2$, although the expanded design matrix no longer has full column rank if the original matrix was already full rank.

More generally, equality occurs whenever the additional variable fails to reduce the minimum residual sum of squares.

This result reveals an important limitation of ordinary $R^2$ as a model-comparison criterion. **Adding explanatory variables can never decrease the in-sample $R^2$**, even when the additional variables do not improve predictions for new observations.

Consequently, a larger $R^2$ does not necessarily imply better predictive performance.

***

### Connection to the Geometric Interpretation

The two derivations in this section express the same decomposition from different perspectives.

The first uses the orthogonality of the residual vector to the fitted values and the intercept column. The second uses the projection matrices associated with the full and intercept-only models.

Because the column space of the intercept-only model is contained in the column space of the full model, the matrices also satisfy

$$
\mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}_0
=
\mathbf{H}_0\mathbf{H}
=
\mathbf{H}_0.
$$

Consequently,

$$
(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)^2
=
\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0.
$$

Thus, $\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0$ is itself a symmetric, idempotent matrix. In particular,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1}
=
(\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H}_0)\mathbf{y}.
$$

The decomposition

$$
\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}
=
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\bar y\mathbf{1})
+
\hat{\mathbf{e}}
$$

therefore separates the total centered response vector into two orthogonal components.

Their squared lengths are $SS_{reg}$ and $SS_{res}$, and the squared length of their sum is $SS_{tot}$.

This provides the connection to the geometric interpretation of multiple regression developed in the following section.


### Uncentered $R^2$: Regression Without an Intercept

The usual definition of $R^2$ compares the residual sum of squares of a regression model with that of the intercept-only model,

$$
y_i=\beta_0+e_i.
$$

When the full model includes an intercept, the intercept-only model is a special case: we can recover it by setting all explanatory-variable coefficients equal to zero. Consequently, the full model cannot have a larger minimum residual sum of squares.

However, consider a regression model **without an intercept**,

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\mathbf{e},
$$

where $\mathbf{X}$ contains only explanatory-variable columns. The intercept-only model is no longer necessarily a special case of this model, since $\mathbf{1}$ need not belong to $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$.

Therefore, the residual sum of squares of the regression model may exceed $SS_{tot}$, and the usual centered $R^2$ may be negative.

Instead, we can compare the regression model with the simplest possible prediction: predicting zero for every observation. This reference model has no parameters to estimate, so its optimization problem is trivial:

$$
\min_{\mathbf{v}\in\{\mathbf{0}\}}
\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{v}\|^2
=
\|\mathbf{y}\|^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2.
$$

Unlike the intercept-only model, the zero prediction is always available to a regression model without an intercept by setting $\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0}$.

```{definition, def-mlr-uncentered-r-squared, name="Uncentered Coefficient of Determination"}
Suppose that the regression model does not include an intercept and that $\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}>0$.

The **Uncentered Coefficient of Determination** is defined as

$$
R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2
=
1-
\frac{SS_{res}}{\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}},
$$

where

$$
SS_{res}
=
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2.
$$

Thus, uncentered $R^2$ measures the proportional reduction in squared error relative to predicting zero for every observation.
```

The use of the zero prediction as a reference allows us to establish the range of uncentered $R^2$ without requiring an intercept.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-uncentered-r-squared-range, name="Range of Uncentered R-Squared"}
Suppose that $\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}>0$. Then the uncentered coefficient of determination satisfies

$$
\boxed{
0\leq R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2\leq 1.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-uncentered-r-squared-range}
The residual sum of squares is the minimum value of the least-squares objective,

$$
SS_{res}
=
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2.
$$

Notice that $\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{0}$ is always a feasible choice, which produces the zero prediction. Therefore,

\begin{align*}
SS_{res}
  &=
  \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2
  \\
  &\leq
  \|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{0}\|^2
  \\
  &=
  \mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Since squared norms are nonnegative,

$$
0\leq SS_{res}\leq\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}.
$$

Dividing by $\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}>0$, we obtain

$$
0
\leq
\frac{SS_{res}}{\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}}
\leq
1.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\boxed{
0\leq R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2\leq 1.
}
$$
```

</details>


**Geometric interpretation.** The least-squares residuals remain orthogonal to the fitted values even without an intercept. Therefore, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\|\mathbf{y}\|^2
=
\|\hat{\mathbf{y}}\|^2
+
\|\hat{\mathbf{e}}\|^2.
$$

Hence, the uncentered coefficient of determination can also be expressed as

$$
\boxed{
R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2
=
\frac{\hat{\mathbf{y}}'\hat{\mathbf{y}}}
{\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}}.
}
$$

This differs from centered $R^2$, which measures improvement relative to predicting the sample mean. Consequently, centered and uncentered $R^2$ should not be compared directly when evaluating different models.

As with ordinary $R^2$, adding explanatory variables cannot decrease uncentered $R^2$ when the same observations are used, since the additional variables enlarge the set of possible fitted values. This does not guarantee better predictions for new observations.

***

### Adjusted $R^2$

We established that adding an explanatory variable cannot increase the residual sum of squares. Consequently, ordinary $R^2$ cannot decrease when explanatory variables are added, even if the additional variables provide very little improvement in fit.

This motivates a modification of $R^2$ that accounts for the number of coefficients in the regression model.

Consider a multiple linear regression model with $p$ explanatory variables and an intercept. Assume that its design matrix $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank and that $n>p+1$.

The column space of $\mathbf{X}$ has dimension $p+1$. Consequently, the residuals belong to its orthogonal complement, which has dimension

$$
n-(p+1)=n-p-1.
$$

The residual sum of squares therefore has $n-p-1$ **residual degrees of freedom**. Similarly, the total sum of squares is based on deviations from the sample mean and has $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

Instead of comparing the original sums of squares, we can compare them after dividing by their respective degrees of freedom.

```{definition, def-mlr-adjusted-r-squared, name="Adjusted Coefficient of Determination"}
Suppose that a multiple linear regression model includes an intercept, has $p$ explanatory variables, and satisfies $n>p+1$ and $SS_{tot}>0$.

The **Adjusted Coefficient of Determination** is defined as

$$
\boxed{
R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2
=
1-
\frac{SS_{res}/(n-p-1)}
{SS_{tot}/(n-1)}.
}
$$

Equivalently, using the ordinary coefficient of determination,

$$
\boxed{
R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2
=
1-
\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}(1-R^2).
}
$$
```

Unlike ordinary $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$ accounts for the number of explanatory variables through the residual degrees of freedom. A new variable must provide a sufficient reduction in residual sum of squares to offset the loss of one degree of freedom.

Since

$$
\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\geq 1,
$$

we also have

$$
R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2\leq R^2\leq 1.
$$

Adjusted $R^2$ can be negative, particularly when the model provides little improvement over the intercept-only model relative to the number of explanatory variables included.

***

#### Adding an Explanatory Variable

We can establish precisely when adding another explanatory variable improves adjusted $R^2$.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-additional-variable-adjusted-r2, name="Effect of Adding an Explanatory Variable on Adjusted R-Squared"}
Consider a regression model with an intercept, $p$ explanatory variables, and residual sum of squares $SS_{res}$.

Suppose that adding one explanatory variable produces a full-column-rank model with residual sum of squares $SS_{res,+}$. Assume that both models use the same observations, $SS_{tot}>0$, and $n>p+2$.

Then adjusted $R^2$ increases if and only if

$$
\boxed{
SS_{res}-SS_{res,+}
>
\frac{SS_{res}}{n-p-1}.
}
$$

Thus, the reduction in residual sum of squares must exceed the original residual sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom.
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-additional-variable-adjusted-r2}
The original model has $n-p-1$ residual degrees of freedom, while the expanded model has $n-p-2$.

Because both models use the same response observations, their total sum of squares is identical. Therefore,

\begin{align*}
R_{\mathrm{adj},+}^2>R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2
&\iff
1-\frac{SS_{res,+}/(n-p-2)}{SS_{tot}/(n-1)}
>
1-\frac{SS_{res}/(n-p-1)}{SS_{tot}/(n-1)}
\\
&\iff
\frac{SS_{res,+}}{n-p-2}
<
\frac{SS_{res}}{n-p-1}
\\
&\iff
(n-p-1)SS_{res,+}
<
(n-p-2)SS_{res}
\\
&\iff
SS_{res}-SS_{res,+}
>
\frac{SS_{res}}{n-p-1}.
\end{align*}

This establishes the result.
```

</details>

Ordinary $R^2$ increases whenever an additional variable reduces the residual sum of squares. Adjusted $R^2$, in contrast, increases only when that reduction exceeds the threshold established above.

**Adjusted $R^2$ is therefore useful for comparing models with different numbers of explanatory variables**, provided they are fitted to the same response observations. However, it remains an in-sample measure of fit. A higher adjusted $R^2$ does not guarantee better predictions on new observations; cross-validation provides a more direct way to evaluate predictive performance.


***


### Summary

The coefficient of determination, $R^2$, measures the reduction in squared error achieved by a regression model relative to a reference prediction. The appropriate reference depends on whether the model includes an intercept.

**1. Regression with an intercept**

The reference is the intercept-only model, which predicts $\bar y$ for every observation. The sum-of-squares decomposition gives

$$
SS_{tot}=SS_{reg}+SS_{res}.
$$

Consequently, the multiple coefficient of determination is

$$
\boxed{
R^2
=
\frac{SS_{reg}}{SS_{tot}}
=
1-\frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}.
}
$$

Provided that $SS_{tot}>0$, we have

$$
0\leq R^2\leq 1.
$$

**2. Regression without an intercept**

The intercept-only model is no longer necessarily contained in the regression model. Instead, uncentered $R^2$ uses the zero prediction as its reference:

$$
\boxed{
R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2
=
1-
\frac{SS_{res}}{\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}}.
}
$$

Since the zero prediction is always available by setting all coefficients equal to zero, we have

$$
0\leq R_{\mathrm{unc}}^2\leq 1,
$$

provided that $\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}>0$.

The usual centered expression, $1-SS_{res}/SS_{tot}$, can be negative for a model without an intercept because its residual sum of squares may exceed that of the intercept-only model.

**3. Interpretation and model comparison**

Both definitions compare the fitted regression model against a reference prediction, but they use different references. Consequently, centered and uncentered $R^2$ should not be compared directly.

An important property of least squares is that adding explanatory variables cannot increase the minimum residual sum of squares. Therefore, when the same observations and reference prediction are used, adding explanatory variables cannot decrease $R^2$.

However, **a higher $R^2$ does not necessarily imply better predictive performance**. It measures improvement in fit to the observations used to estimate the model. To evaluate predictions for new observations, we can instead use methods such as cross-validation.

































## Geometric Interpretation of Multiple Linear Regression

Multiple linear regression can be interpreted geometrically as projecting the response vector $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of the design matrix $\mathbf{X}$.

The fitted-value vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, while the residual vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is orthogonal to this column space.

The following diagram illustrates this interpretation and its connection to the sum-of-squares decomposition.

```{r geo-int, echo=FALSE}
par(mar = c(0,0,0,0))
plot(NULL,
     xlim = c(0,100),
     ylim = c(0,100),
     xaxt = "n",
     yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "",
     ylab = "")
xPad <- 20
yPad <- 50
polygon(x = c(0, xPad, 100, 100 - xPad, 0),
        y = c(0, yPad, yPad,         0, 0),
        col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.2),
        border = NA)
segments(x0  = xPad,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 10,
         y0  = yPad,
         y1  = 100 - 10,
         lwd = 2)
segments(x0  = 100 - xPad - 10,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 10,
         y0  = 100 - 10,
         y1  = yPad - 20,
         lwd = 2,
         col = 'red')
segments(x0  = xPad,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 10,
         y0  = yPad,
         y1  = yPad - 20,
         lwd = 2)
segments(x0  = xPad,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 30,

segments(x0  = 100 - xPad - 10,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 30,

segments(x0  = 100 - xPad - 13,
         x1  = 100 - xPad - 13,
         y0  = yPad - 23,

         lwd = 2,
         col = 'blue')
segments(x0  = 100 - xPad - 13,

text(x = 35,

text(x = 35,
     y = 50,
     labels = expression(hat(y)))
text(x = 35,

text(x      = 64,

```

The diagram represents the following vectors and subspaces:

- $\mathbf{y}$ is the observed response vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
- The gray plane represents the column space $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$, a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
- $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$.
- $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0=\bar y\mathbf{1}$ is the fitted-value vector from the intercept-only model. Since $\mathbf{X}$ includes an intercept, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0$ also belongs to $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$.

The three vectors

$$
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0,
\qquad
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0
$$

form a right triangle.

To see why, notice that both $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0$ belong to $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$. Therefore,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0
\in
\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X}).
$$

From the properties of least squares, we know that the residual vector is orthogonal to every vector in this column space. Consequently,

$$
\underbrace{
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
}_{\hat{\mathbf{e}}}'
\underbrace{
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0)
}_{\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})}
=
0.
$$

Thus, the residual vector and the difference between the two fitted-value vectors are perpendicular. Applying the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\left\|
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0
\right\|^2
=
\left\|
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}
\right\|^2
+
\left\|
\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0
\right\|^2.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0)'
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0)
&=
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})'
(\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})
\\
&\quad+
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0)'
(\hat{\mathbf{y}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0=\bar y\mathbf{1}$, this is precisely the sum-of-squares decomposition established in the previous section:

$$
\boxed{
SS_{tot}=SS_{res}+SS_{reg}.
}
$$

The geometric interpretation therefore shows that the decomposition is a direct consequence of orthogonal projection, regardless of the number of explanatory variables in the model, provided that an intercept is included.

***































## Centered and Standardized Variables

Centering and standardization extend naturally from simple linear regression to multiple linear regression. They are particularly useful because they provide alternative expressions for the least-squares coefficients in terms of sample covariances and correlations.

Throughout this section, we use the notation

$$
\mathbf{X}_*
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1 & \mathbf{x}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{x}_p
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}
$$

for the matrix containing only the explanatory variables. The complete design matrix is

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(p+1)}.
$$

This distinction is useful because the intercept column should not be centered or standardized.

***

### Centered Variables

Let

$$
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\bar x_1\\
\bar x_2\\
\vdots\\
\bar x_p
\end{bmatrix}
$$

denote the vector containing the sample mean of each explanatory variable. Since

$$
\bar x_j
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{x}_j,
$$

we can write

\begin{align*}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&=
\frac{1}{n}
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_1'\mathbf{1}\\
\mathbf{x}_2'\mathbf{1}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{x}_p'\mathbf{1}
\end{bmatrix}
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1}.
\end{align*}

The centered explanatory-variable matrix is obtained by subtracting the corresponding column mean from every observation:

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}
&=
\mathbf{X}_*-\mathbf{1}\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*
-
\mathbf{1}
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1}
\right)'
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*
-
\frac{1}{n}
\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{X}_*
\\
&=
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)\mathbf{X}_*.
\end{align*}

This motivates the centering matrix.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-centering-matrix, name="Centering Matrix"}
Define

$$
\mathbf{C}
=
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
=
\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_0,
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{H}_0
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
$$

is the projection matrix associated with the intercept-only model.

Then:

1. $\mathbf{C}$ is symmetric,
2. $\mathbf{C}$ is idempotent,
3. $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0}$, and
4. for any matrix $\mathbf{A}$ with $n$ rows, $\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}$ subtracts the column mean from every column of $\mathbf{A}$.

In particular,

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}
=
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{y}_c
=
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-centering-matrix}
First,

$$
\mathbf{C}'
=
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)'
=
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
=
\mathbf{C},
$$

so $\mathbf{C}$ is symmetric.

Also,

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{C}^2
&=
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)^2
\\
&=
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
+
\frac{1}{n^2}
\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\\
&=
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{2}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
+
\frac{1}{n}
\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\\
&=
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\\
&=
\mathbf{C},
\end{align*}

where we used $\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1}=n$. Thus, $\mathbf{C}$ is idempotent.

Similarly,

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{1}
&=
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)\mathbf{1}
\\
&=
\mathbf{1}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}
(\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1})
\\
&=
\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{1}
\\
&=
\mathbf{0}.
\end{align*}

Finally, if $\mathbf{A}$ has $n$ rows, then

$$
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{A}
$$

contains the means of its columns. Therefore,

$$
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}
=
\mathbf{A}
-
\mathbf{1}
\left(
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{A}
\right)
$$

subtracts the corresponding mean from each column.
```

</details>

***

### Sample Covariance

Using the centered explanatory variables, define the sample covariance matrix

$$
\mathbf{S}_{XX}
\in
\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}
$$

by

$$
\mathbf{S}_{XX}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{X}_{*,c}.
$$

Its $(j,k)$ entry is the sample covariance between explanatory variables $\mathbf{x}_j$ and $\mathbf{x}_k$.

Similarly, define the covariance vector between the explanatory variables and the response as

$$
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{y}_c
\in
\mathbb{R}^{p}.
$$

The centering matrix gives several useful equivalent expressions.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-covariance-identities, name="Covariance Identities"}
The sample covariance matrix satisfies

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{S}_{XX}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{X}_*
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_{*,c}.
}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{y}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}_c.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-covariance-identities}
Since

$$
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}
=
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*,
$$

we have

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{X}_{*,c}
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*,
\end{align*}

because $\mathbf{C}$ is symmetric and idempotent.

Also,

$$
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*
=
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{X}_*
=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_{*,c}.
$$

The covariance vector follows in the same way:

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{y}_c
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

$$
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{X}_{*,c}'\mathbf{y}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}_c.
$$
```

</details>

Thus, for the covariance calculation, centering either side is sufficient because multiplication by the centering matrix removes the corresponding mean automatically.

***

### Least-Squares Coefficients in Covariance Form

We now use the covariance quantities to obtain an alternative expression for the multiple regression coefficients.

Write the coefficient vector as

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat\beta_0\\
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

where

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat\beta_1\\
\vdots\\
\hat\beta_p
\end{bmatrix}
$$

contains the coefficients associated with the explanatory variables.

Since the complete design matrix is

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix},
$$

the usual least-squares solution is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}.
$$

The covariance representation follows by explicitly evaluating this expression.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-coefficients-covariance, name="Regression Coefficients in Covariance Form"}
Suppose that the design matrix

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}
$$

has full column rank.

Then the estimated coefficients associated with the explanatory variables satisfy

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
=
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-coefficients-covariance}
We begin from

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}.
$$

Since

$$
\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1}'\\
\mathbf{X}_*'
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1} & \mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}
\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1}
&
\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{X}_*
\\
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1}
&
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}

Because

$$
\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{1}=n
$$

and

$$
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
=
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1},
$$

we obtain

$$
\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
n
&
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\\
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_*
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To invert this matrix, use the block-matrix inverse with upper-left block $n$. The corresponding Schur complement is

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_*
-
(n\bar{\mathbf{x}})
n^{-1}
(n\bar{\mathbf{x}}')
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_*
-
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{X}_*
-
\frac{1}{n}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{X}_*
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)
\mathbf{X}_*
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*
\\
&=
(n-1)\mathbf{S}_{XX}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{n}
+
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\bigl((n-1)\mathbf{S}_{XX}\bigr)^{-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&
\displaystyle
-\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\bigl((n-1)\mathbf{S}_{XX}\bigr)^{-1}
\\[8pt]
\displaystyle
-\bigl((n-1)\mathbf{S}_{XX}\bigr)^{-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&
\displaystyle
\bigl((n-1)\mathbf{S}_{XX}\bigr)^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}
\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{n}
+
\frac{1}{n-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&
\displaystyle
-\frac{1}{n-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\\[8pt]
\displaystyle
-\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
&
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}

Also,

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{y}\\
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
\end{bmatrix}
\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
n\bar y\\
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align*}

Multiplying the second row-block gives

\begin{align*}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
&=
-\frac{n\bar y}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\bar{\mathbf{x}}
+
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\left(
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
-
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar y
\right).
\end{align*}

Now,

\begin{align*}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
-
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar y
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
-
\frac{1}{n}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'
\left(
\mathbf{I}
-
\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}'
\right)
\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
(n-1)\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
\end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
&=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
(n-1)\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
\\
&=
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
\end{align*}

Hence,

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
=
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
}
$$
```

</details>

This expression separates two components of the multiple-regression problem:

- $\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}$ incorporates the relationships among the explanatory variables.
- $\mathbf{S}_{Xy}$ incorporates the relationships between the explanatory variables and the response.

Thus, unlike simple linear regression, each coefficient depends not only on the relationship between one explanatory variable and the response, but also on how the explanatory variables relate to one another.

***

### The Intercept and the Effect of Centering

The corresponding intercept estimate also has a convenient covariance-form expression.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-intercept-covariance, name="Intercept Estimate"}
Under the assumptions of the previous proposition,

$$
\boxed{
\hat\beta_0
=
\bar y
-
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}.
}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\hat\beta_0
=
\bar y
-
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-intercept-covariance}
Using the first row-block of the block-matrix expression,

\begin{align*}
\hat\beta_0
&=
\bar y
+
\frac{n\bar y}{n-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}
-
\frac{1}{n-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
\\
&=
\bar y
-
\frac{1}{n-1}
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\left(
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
-
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar y
\right).
\end{align*}

From the previous proof,

$$
\mathbf{X}_*'\mathbf{y}
-
n\bar{\mathbf{x}}\bar y
=
(n-1)\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
$$

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
\hat\beta_0
&=
\bar y
-
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
\\
&=
\bar y
-
\bar{\mathbf{x}}'
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}.
\end{align*}
```

</details>

These results also clarify what happens when variables are centered.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-centering-coefficients, name="Effect of Centering on the Regression Coefficients"}
Suppose the regression model includes an intercept.

1. Centering the explanatory variables does not change their estimated coefficients.

2. If only the explanatory variables are centered, the estimated intercept becomes

$$
\boxed{
\hat\beta_{0,c}=\bar y.
}
$$

3. If both the explanatory variables and the response are centered, the estimated intercept becomes

$$
\boxed{
\hat\beta_{0,c}=0.
}
$$

In the third case, fitting the centered variables without an intercept produces the same slope estimates and fitted centered values as fitting them with an intercept.
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-centering-coefficients}
Centering does not change the covariance matrix or covariance vector:

$$
\mathbf{S}_{X_cX_c}
=
\mathbf{S}_{XX},
\qquad
\mathbf{S}_{X_cy}
=
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0,c}
=
\mathbf{S}_{X_cX_c}^{-1}
\mathbf{S}_{X_cy}
=
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}
=
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}.
$$

If the explanatory variables are centered, their mean vector is $\mathbf{0}$. Hence,

$$
\hat\beta_{0,c}
=
\bar y
-
\mathbf{0}'
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
=
\bar y.
$$

If the response is also centered, then $\bar y_c=0$, and therefore

$$
\hat\beta_{0,c}
=
0.
$$

Thus, when both the response and explanatory variables are centered, the intercept estimated by a model that includes one is exactly zero. Removing the intercept in this centered problem therefore leaves the slope estimates unchanged.
```

</details>

The last statement applies specifically to the regression of the **centered response on the centered explanatory variables**. It does not imply that an intercept can generally be omitted from a regression on the original, uncentered variables.

***

### Standardized Variables

Centering removes location. Standardization additionally rescales each variable by its sample standard deviation.

Assume that every explanatory variable has positive sample variance. Define

$$
\mathbf{D}_X
=
\begin{bmatrix}
S_{x_1x_1}^{-1/2} & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
0 & S_{x_2x_2}^{-1/2} & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & \cdots & S_{x_px_p}^{-1/2}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The standardized explanatory-variable matrix is

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf{X}_s
=
\mathbf{X}_{*,c}\mathbf{D}_X
=
\mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}_*\mathbf{D}_X.
}
$$

Thus, the $j$th column of $\mathbf{X}_s$ is

$$
\frac{\mathbf{x}_j-\bar x_j\mathbf{1}}
{\sqrt{S_{x_jx_j}}}.
$$

The matrix $\mathbf{C}$ acts on the rows and can center any matrix with $n$ rows. In contrast, $\mathbf{D}_X$ acts on the columns and is specific to the standard deviations of the explanatory variables in $\mathbf{X}_*$.

Similarly, if $S_{yy}>0$, the standardized response is

$$
\mathbf{y}_s
=
\frac{\mathbf{y}-\bar y\mathbf{1}}
{\sqrt{S_{yy}}}.
$$

Because standardized variables are centered, their sample means are zero.

***

### Sample Correlation Matrix

The sample correlation matrix of the explanatory variables is defined by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{XX}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{X}_s.
$$

Its $(j,k)$ entry is

$$
[\mathbf{r}_{XX}]_{jk}
=
\frac{S_{x_jx_k}}
{\sqrt{S_{x_jx_j}S_{x_kx_k}}},
$$

the sample correlation between explanatory variables $\mathbf{x}_j$ and $\mathbf{x}_k$.

Similarly, define the sample correlation vector between the explanatory variables and the response as

$$
\mathbf{r}_{Xy}
=
\frac{1}{n-1}
\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{y}_s.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\mathbf{r}_{XX}
=
\mathbf{D}_X
\mathbf{S}_{XX}
\mathbf{D}_X,
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{r}_{Xy}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{S_{yy}}}
\mathbf{D}_X
\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
$$

***

### Regression with Standardized Variables

Since both $\mathbf{X}_s$ and $\mathbf{y}_s$ are centered, fitting the standardized regression with an intercept produces an estimated intercept of zero. Consequently, the same slope estimates can be obtained by fitting

$$
\mathbf{y}_s
=
\mathbf{X}_s\boldsymbol{\beta}_s
+
\mathbf{e}_s
$$

without explicitly including an intercept.

```{proposition, prp-mlr-standardized-coefficients, name="Regression Coefficients for Standardized Variables"}
Suppose that $\mathbf{r}_{XX}$ is invertible. The least-squares coefficients from the regression of the standardized response on the standardized explanatory variables satisfy

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_s
=
\mathbf{r}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{r}_{Xy}.
}
$$
```

<details><summary><span style="color:green">Proof</span></summary>

```{proof, pro-mlr-standardized-coefficients}
The least-squares solution is

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_s
=
(\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{X}_s)^{-1}
\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{y}_s.
$$

From the definitions of the sample correlation matrix and correlation vector,

$$
\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{X}_s
=
(n-1)\mathbf{r}_{XX}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{X}_s'\mathbf{y}_s
=
(n-1)\mathbf{r}_{Xy}.
$$

Therefore,

\begin{align*}
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_s
&=
\left(
(n-1)\mathbf{r}_{XX}
\right)^{-1}
(n-1)\mathbf{r}_{Xy}
\\
&=
\mathbf{r}_{XX}^{-1}
\mathbf{r}_{Xy}.
\end{align*}
```

</details>

This result is the standardized analogue of

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-0}
=
\mathbf{S}_{XX}^{-1}\mathbf{S}_{Xy}.
$$

For the original variables, the slope coefficients depend on the covariance structure. For standardized variables, they depend on the corresponding correlation structure.

Because standardized variables are unitless and each has sample standard deviation one, the magnitudes of their coefficients are more directly comparable than coefficients measured on different physical scales. However, coefficient magnitude should not by itself be interpreted as a measure of variable importance. The coefficients still depend on the relationships among all explanatory variables through $\mathbf{r}_{XX}^{-1}$.

***

### Example: GDP Data

We can verify these results using the GDP data introduced earlier.

The notation used in the R code differs slightly from the mathematical notation above:
